Indigenous languages of the Americas. The languages spoken by the diverse pre-Columbian civilizations and their descendants, ranging from large language families like Quechua with eight or more million speakers and Navajo with one hundred eighty thousand or more speakers to dozens of undocumented or nearly extinct language isolates. These languages exhibit remarkable structural diversity—polysynthetic verb systems, ergative-absolutive alignment, complex tone systems—and encode unique knowledge about botany, astronomy, and oral history that is lost when speakers shift to Spanish, Portuguese, or English.

The Americas contain unprecedented linguistic diversity. Pre-Columbian populations spoke thousands of distinct languages organized into hundreds of language families—far more diversity than Europe. Major language families include Quechuan in the Andes, Aymaran in the southern Andes, Oto-Manguean in Mexico, Oto-Pamean, Athabaskan in North America, Salishan in the Pacific Northwest, and hundreds of isolated languages with no documented relatives. Franz Boas pioneered documentation of indigenous North American languages like Kwakwaka'wakw, Bella Coola, and Chinook. His work established that non-European languages possessed complex grammar and disproved racist hierarchies of linguistic primitiveness.

Spanish and Portuguese conquest triggered rapid language death. Colonial language policy suppressed indigenous languages in favor of European languages, literacy, and Christian education. Navajo and Quechua are exceptional successes. Both maintained large speaker bases and achieved official or co-official status in their nations, partly through deliberate cultural revitalization and educational policies. Indigenous American languages exhibit typological extremes. Navajo is highly polysynthetic, with one verb able to express an entire sentence, while Pirahã is renowned for minimal numerals and alleged absence of recursion, disputed by many linguists.

Many indigenous language communities lack orthographies, educational materials, or institutional support. Documentation by linguists is often the only record preventing complete extinction.
